title: The Whole Thing at Once
logline: A twelfth-century reservoir so large it was named as a sea, which is not one body of water at all, and which the authorities count as five and as three, both correctly, and which can only be seen either way from the air.
human_question: If the same thing can be honestly counted as five or as three depending on where you stand and how much of it is showing, what am I actually pointing at when I use its name?

place.what_kind_of_place: A very large, very shallow artificial reservoir on the western side of a ruined medieval royal capital in the dry zone, held by an earth bund about fourteen kilometres long and up to roughly twelve metres high, pierced by ancient stone sluices that have been repaired and re-fitted many times over. It is not one basin. It was made in the twelfth century by joining separate older reservoirs to each other with narrow channels, and the banks between them still exist: a couple of them surface as low pale lines across the water and become exposed embankments when the level drops. At the southern end the bund runs past a ruined monastic library complex and a colossal rock-cut figure on the shore. The north end sits under the walls of the old citadel, so the water has a ruined city on one shoulder and open dry-zone scrub and paddy on the other.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Scale, and a scale that changes. At full supply it is an inland horizon: twenty-odd square kilometres of water with a flat rim, a metal sheet at sunset, thousands of waterbirds working the shallows, and the towers and dagabas of a dead capital standing in the trees along one shore. Then the dry months take metres off it and the same place becomes a landscape of exposed banks, cracked grey margins, stumps and channels — and the thing that was one sheet of water is visibly three. The bund gives fourteen kilometres of continuous elevated line to fly and walk, with stone sluices set into it that carry eight centuries of patching in one frame. And the payoff shot is free and repeatable: a high frame that holds the whole of it, in which the joins are visible, which nobody standing on the bank can have.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The water level, on the irrigation year's schedule, and everything that follows it. The reservoir fills through the north-east monsoon and is drawn down through the cultivation season until the shallow arms are mud and the internal banks stand clear. Birds arrive and thin out with the shallows. Sluices are opened and closed and the released water goes out through channels into paddy east of the bund. Light does the rest: the dry-zone haze burns off through the morning and comes back in the afternoon, and at last light the whole sheet goes to metal and then to nothing. None of it is under the crew's control and none of it needs to be.
place.when_it_looks_best: Two trips, and the film needs both. Around February to April, at and after full supply, for the single unbroken sheet, the metal sunsets and the birds. Then August into September, at the bottom of the drawdown, for the exposed internal banks, the cracked margins and the shot in which one sheet of water has become three basins. Early morning for a clear high frame before the haze builds; the hour before sunset for the bund, the sluices and the southern end. Full moon nights are worth a test for the still water and the ruins, but nothing in the film depends on them.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A big-water film with a hard shape to it. An inland sea at dawn with a dead city on its shore; fourteen kilometres of earth bund flown end to end; ancient stone sluices opened and water running out into paddy; a hundred thousand birds in the shallows; a metal sunset behind a ruined rotunda and a figure cut out of rock. Then the same place with the water pulled back, cracked mud and old banks standing up out of it, and the final lift that shows what the first shot promised. Someone who never hears a word of the narration gets a complete piece: full, drawn down, and seen whole at the end.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes a demonstration about counting. The voice never claims anything the frame does not already contain: a name that says sea over a thing that is not one; two official counts, five and three, both correct and both invisible from the bank; a bank of earth that exists only because heat, cold, water and repair are constantly acting on it; and a lift at the end that names the one reality nothing in the film can show. The chronicle's famous sentence about rainwater is used as evidence of what somebody intended, and then put down. Nobody's greatness is the subject and no engineering is being admired.

sequence.on_screen: First light. The drone lifts off the earth bund on the eastern side and keeps climbing until the frame stops changing: one sheet of water filling the lower half of the image, the towers of a ruined city standing out of the trees on the near shore, and two faint pale lines running out across the water where old banks come up to the surface.
sequence.voice: The name given to this place calls it a sea. It is not a sea, and it is not one body of water either. It was made by joining separate reservoirs to each other with narrow cuts, and those two pale lines are where the banks between them still are. Stand anywhere on the shore and they do not exist.

sequence.on_screen: Higher, and the drone turns slowly so the whole expanse passes through the frame from end to end. Then a hold on one of the necks: a gap in an old submerged bank with water moving through it, weed lying along the current.
sequence.voice: Count the reservoirs that were joined and the answer is five. Count the basins that hold water together now and the answer is three. Both counts are in official print. Neither is a mistake. They are counting different things, or the same thing at different dates. One name sits on top of both of them.

sequence.on_screen: Down on the bund at water level, lens almost on the surface. A flat horizon, fishing stakes standing in the shallows, egrets working a snag, the far shore a grey line. Nothing in the frame says how many pieces of water are in front of the camera.
sequence.voice: From here neither count is available to you. There is one sheet of water and one horizon and that is the whole offer. The old definition of a mind is nearly as narrow as that. Knowing, always of something, one thing at a time, and never arriving at all unless there is something to know. Whatever is out there, you are handed one of it.

sequence.on_screen: The bund itself: fourteen kilometres of piled earth flown end to end in one move, then down among the stone sluices, close on cut stone, brick patching, iron, a modern gate bolted into an ancient opening, water going out through it into a channel.
sequence.voice: The chronicle the monks kept puts one sentence in the mouth of the king who had this made: that not even a little of the water that comes from the rain should reach the sea without first being made useful. That is evidence of an intention. It is not a moral, and it did not make him a great man. What it made was this. Earth carried and piled. Stone cut. Holes left in the bank on purpose. These books define physical stuff by what is done to it rather than by what it is — the kind of thing that gets knocked about and altered by heat and by cold. A wall of earth holding water back is that definition with a camera on it.

sequence.on_screen: The dry months. The water has pulled metres back from the tree line: a wide margin of cracked grey mud with stumps in it, heat shimmer. Then the high frame again, and now the sheet is plainly three basins, divided by exposed banks that were underwater in February.
sequence.voice: And here is what decides the count. At full supply this reads as one. Take a few metres off it and the banks come up and it is obviously three. Nothing was added to it and nothing was taken away. You could simply see more of it.

sequence.on_screen: Low and slow over one of the necks, following the water through the gap and out the far side in a single unbroken move with no cut in it.
sequence.voice: That was one move over one body of water, and it was not. It was held, let go, held again. These books say something very close to that about a mind, and they say it in two ways that must never be run together. One says a mind is one thing in its general nature and is only divided up so that it can be taught. The other says a being does not have one mind at all, but a run of extremely brief separate ones, too fast and too gapless for anybody to catch the joins.

sequence.on_screen: The southern end. A road running along an embankment, and on the far side of it two shallow depressions with scrub and paddy in them and the outlines of old banks still legible in the ground. A culvert. Nothing dramatic.
sequence.voice: Two of the five are on the other side of that road. A repair sent the water the wrong way, a temporary dam was thrown up to stop it, the dam became a road, and when the rehabilitations were done in the last century those two were left out. The count settled at three. The map these books hand their own student has a gap just as honest. One of them counts eighty-one ordinary kinds of mind plus eight and gets eighty-nine. The other counts four regions — fifty-four, fifteen, twelve and forty — and gets a hundred and twenty-one, and never writes eighty-nine down anywhere at all. The simple addition that gets you from one total to the other is printed in neither of them. Somebody assembled it, and now everybody quotes it.

sequence.on_screen: Last light at the southern shore: the ruined rotunda and vestibule of the old library complex, and the great rock-cut figure above the water, both black against a sheet going to metal. Then a slow lift until the whole thing is in one frame again, and a hold until the light has gone out of it.
sequence.voice: Three of the four things these books call real are made. They come together, they hold for a while, they come apart. Everything in this film is that kind of thing, including the name and including both counts. The fourth is not made. It is not this water and it is not the quiet and it is not the dark, and there is no shot of it here or in any film. On the map it is one word, and there is nothing under it that a camera can reach.

concept_merge.why_together: C018 is the concept of a classification held in one view, and the two totals are its whole point: Pradeepika states eighty-one mundane plus eight supramundane making eighty-nine, or a hundred and twenty-one when the supramundane are counted by the five levels of absorption [C018-P:L23–L27], and closes the chapter with a full-page chart that gathers every type into a single frame [C018-P:L33–L56]; Margaya reaches a hundred and twenty-one instead from four spheres [C018-M:L125] and tells the student to learn the list by heart because further study depends on it [C018-M:L3]. The digest's own reading is that eighty-nine and a hundred and twenty-one are not a disagreement but the same set counted at two resolutions, the eight becoming forty when the depth of absorption is counted as well [C018-P:L23–L25; C018-M:L119–L123]. C003 is what such a map is a map of: mind defined as the knowing of an object, arising only in dependence on an object, taking one object at a time, and running as a beginningless stream of extremely brief moments that passes for a single continuous mind [C003-P:L25; C003-P:L33; C003-P:L31]. C002 is the frame around both: everything falls into four ultimate realities described as activities or forces rather than substances [C002-P:L34; C002-M:L3], materiality being defined by what opposing conditions such as heat and cold do to it [C002-P:L40; C002-M:L17], three of the four conditioned and impermanent and the fourth not produced at all [C002-M:L21]. This reservoir is the only kind of place where all three are standing in the landscape at once and at a scale one frame can hold: a single name that says sea, a documented count of five and a documented count of three, and a structure whose count depends on how much of it the water is currently showing you.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the two totals are not arithmetic and not a textual problem, but a fact about resolution — and that a viewer can watch the resolution change. C018 alone is a list, and its own digest warns that a film which dwells on the numbers becomes a lecture. C003 alone is a definition with nothing to look at. C002 alone is a frame with nothing in it. Put on this water they make the film's best two shots do the argument: the high frame in which the joins are visible and the count is available, and the bank-level frame in which there is one horizon and no count is available at all. The history supplies what no analogy could, because it actually happened: the same body of water is five in one authority and three in another, and the reason is a nineteenth-century repair, a temporary dam that turned into a road, and a set of rehabilitations that left two basins out. That is exactly the shape of the digest's own gap — the four-sphere sum that neither source prints [C018-P:L23; C018-P:L21] — and the film keeps both gaps open rather than closing either. The trio also fixes the ending as a refusal: the unmade reality is not on this map and nothing a camera can reach belongs to it [C002-M:L21; C002-P:L46].

concept_links.why: The concept is the whole classification put in one view together with the fact that it has two honest totals. Pradeepika gives eighty-one plus eight for eighty-nine, and a hundred and twenty-one when the supramundane are counted by the five levels of absorption, with sixty-seven of the hundred and twenty-one being absorption consciousnesses [C018-P:L23–L27], and gathers everything into a single full-page chart at the end of the chapter [C018-P:L33–L56]. Margaya never states eighty-nine at all; it arrives at a hundred and twenty-one from four spheres [C018-M:L125] and instructs the student to commit the list to memory because what follows depends on it [C018-M:L3]. This place is that structure standing in the landscape: one name meaning sea, five original reservoirs joined by narrow channels, three interconnected basins counted today, both counts correct because they count different things or the same thing at different dates, and neither count visible except from the air. Four limits from the digest apply and are written into the risks. The types are momentary kinds of consciousness and not personality types. They are not a ladder of better and worse people, and the chart itself shows many of the higher ones accompanied by equanimity rather than joy [C018-P:L27; C018-P:L56]. The supramundane types are tied to the stages of the path and are not peak experiences anyone can switch on [C018-M:L109–L123]. And the arithmetic is not the point [C018-P:L23–L25]; a film that dwells on it becomes a lecture, which is why the numbers are spoken once, in beat 7, and then dropped. One uncertainty is load-bearing and governs that beat: the simple four-sphere sum is printed in neither source, Pradeepika giving only eighty-one plus eight [C018-P:L23] with the derivation of eighty-one lying before the start of the extract [C018-P:L21], so the film may describe the gap but must never put an assembled table on screen as a quotation.

This concept supplies what the map is a map of, and the shot on the bund. Mind is defined as the capacity that knows an object: it arises only in dependence on an object, it takes one object and one aspect of it at a time, and it runs as a beginningless stream of extremely brief moments that feels like a single continuous mind [C003-P:L25; C003-P:L33; C003-P:L31]. That is beat 3, standing at water level with one horizon and no count, and it is beat 6, flying through a neck in one unbroken move over what is not one thing. The digest is explicit that the two sources use 'one' in different senses and that they must not be merged: Margaya says mind is one in its general nature and is divided only for teaching [C003-M:L5], while Pradeepika says a being has not one mind but a stream that merely seems to be one [C003-P:L25]. The film keeps them apart and never lets the aerial settle which sense is meant. Two further limits from the digest bear on this location directly. The author's argument that mind rests on a physical base at the heart rather than in the brain [C003-P:L59–L69] is a commentarial position and must not appear on screen as science. And the ripening simile for resultant consciousness [C003-P:L105–L109] must never be used to explain why a season failed or why any particular field went dry here; the digest rules that out in terms. One further detail earns its place: both sources name the spheres by where such minds 'mostly' arise, not exclusively [C003-M:L11–L19], which is the same loose fit between a name and a plural thing that the reservoir's name has, and the film may note it without pressing it.

This concept gives the film its materiality and its ending. Everything the teaching describes falls into four ultimate realities, described as activities or forces rather than substances and, in Pradeepika's words, as true and existent [C002-P:L27–L30; C002-M:L5; C002-P:L34; C002-M:L3]. Materiality is defined by what opposing conditions such as cold and heat do to it [C002-P:L40; C002-M:L17], which is beat 4: an earth bund and a cut-stone sluice are matter under exactly that description, and Pradeepika's own observation that masses of materiality are what appear to us as trees, rocks and bodies is the ground for a name like sea sitting over an assembled thing. Three of the four are conditioned and impermanent and the fourth is not produced by any cause [C002-M:L21], which is why beat 8 can only name it. The digest's limits are written into the risks and into that beat: it is not relaxation, not a calm mood, not simply death, and it is realised only by noble ones through the supramundane path and great effort [C002-P:L46; C002-M:L21], so still water, dusk and silence are not it. The digest also forbids two slides this film could easily make: 'nothing is real', which Pradeepika's calling the ultimates true existent realities rules out [C002-P:L34], and glossing earth, water, fire and air as literal soil, water, flame and wind, since the extract names the four great elements without defining them [C002-P:L40]. A film standing on an earth dam full of water must not reach for that gloss, and this one does not.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That a count is a fact about how much of a thing is showing and how closely you looked, not a fact about how much of it there is. The same water is five and is three; the same set of mind-moments is eighty-nine and is a hundred and twenty-one. Nothing was added by counting more finely, and the name — which says sea, and covers all of it — was never accurate and was never wrong either.
what_must_be_real: Both counts, with their sources, and the reason they differ: a nineteenth-century repair that sent water the wrong way, a temporary dam that became a permanent road, and rehabilitations that left two of the five basins out. The film records that as layers and does not adjudicate it or turn it into anyone's grievance. The actual state of the reservoir is filmed as it is: siltation, weed, the shallow arms, the condition of the sluices, whatever the level happens to be. No sequence is cut to suggest the water is fuller, or the internal banks clearer, than they were on the day. The chronicle's sentence about rainwater is given as a sentence in a chronicle attributed to a king, not as the king's own words and not as a verified quotation with a verse number the project has not checked. People fishing, washing, working the paddy or visiting the ruins are not exhibits, are not filmed in a way that makes them the subject, and are not approached at all where consent cannot be obtained. No chart or table is put on screen as a quotation from a source if the project assembled it.
position_hint: middle: it is the group's change of scale, and the only film in the slate whose subject is a count rather than a thing named. The whole map is laid out here and the later groups open one region of it at a time. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Letting this become a film about a king's greatness or about medieval engineering genius. The chronicle's sentence is evidence of an intention and nothing more, and the film says so in the beat that uses it.

Letting the arithmetic run the film. The digest states plainly that the numbers are a matter of counting method and that a film which dwells on them becomes a lecture, so the totals are spoken once and dropped.

Putting an assembled table on screen as if it were quoted. The simple four-sphere sum appears in neither source, and Pradeepika's derivation of eighty-one lies outside the extract, so any figure of that kind must be marked as assembled or left out.

Reading the types as personality types, as a ranking of better and worse people, or as peak experiences available with a technique; the digest forbids all three, and the chart itself shows many of the higher types accompanied by equanimity rather than joy.

Merging the two senses of 'one'. One source says mind is one in its general nature and divided only for teaching; the other says a being has not one mind but a stream that seems to be one. The aerial must not be allowed to settle that for the sources.

Implying moral causation about water. A low year here is rainfall, siltation and allocation, and the ripening simile in the digest must never be used to explain a failed field or anyone's circumstances.
Letting the last beat imply that still water, dusk, quiet or a ruin is the unconditioned; the digest rules that out and beat 8 is written to refuse it.
Glossing the four great elements as literal soil, water, flame and wind, which is tempting on an earth dam and which the digest explicitly blocks, since the extract names them without defining them.
Presenting the heart-base argument, or any of that author's physiological claims, as established fact.
Turning a nineteenth- and twentieth-century engineering failure into a colonial-grievance narrative or a nationalist one. It is recorded as what happened and left there.

Drone work over a working irrigation scheme, a World Heritage archaeological zone and people fishing, bathing and farming. Permissions are a real constraint and consent for anyone identifiable is not optional.
Crowds and observance at the ruins on the shore. Visitors and worshippers are not spectacle and are not the film's material.
drop_if: The whole reservoir cannot be held in a single frame at a legal and safe drone height, because the first, fifth and last beats are the film.
Drone permission over the archaeological zone and the irrigation works cannot be obtained, and the high frames would have to be bought in or faked.
The internal banks do not become visible at the bottom of the drawdown in the filming year, so the count cannot be seen to change on screen.
The two counts turn out on closer reading to be one authority's error rather than two honest enumerations, which would remove the film's engine.

connections.note: One mountain with four names that are all correct; one body of water with two counts that are both correct. The same distinction between a name and what it covers, taken from naming to counting.
One film lays the whole map out at once; the other watches a single opening receiving a single arrival.
A run of separate holdings that reads as one continuous thing seen from above, and the same continuity made visible by speed.

selection.reason: The only idea in which a count, rather than a thing named, is the subject, and the only location where a single name, two documented counts and a structure that shows or hides its own divisions with the water level are all in one frame.

review.note: Relocated and rewritten from the ground up. The village tank cascade has been set aside, and the film now stands on the great twelfth-century reservoir on the western side of a ruined medieval royal capital in the dry zone; the place, its district and the names of its basins are given only in suggested_location, as the place-name rule requires. The reasoning that worked in the previous version is kept and made far stronger. C018's point is that eighty-nine and a hundred and twenty-one are the same set counted at two resolutions, and this reservoir is that structure standing in the landscape: it is named as a sea, it is not one body of water, and it is counted two ways in print. Five original wewa, joined to each other by narrow channels, or three interconnected basins today, because a repair in the later nineteenth century sent water the wrong way, the temporary dam thrown up to stop it became a permanent road, and the rehabilitations carried out from 1937 left two of the five out. Both counts are correct; they count different things, or the same thing at different dates; and neither is available from the bank. The film's engine is therefore one name, two honest counts and a high frame as the only place either count exists — reinforced by the fact that the count visibly changes with the drawdown, three basins at low water and one sheet at full supply, so the film's most beautiful shot is also its clearest statement of the concept. The Cūḷavaṃsa's injunction attributed to Parākramabāhu I, that not even a little of the water that comes from the rain should reach the sea without first being made useful, is used strictly as evidence of an intention and explicitly not as a moral or as proof of a king's greatness; that the project has not verified a chapter-and-verse reference, and that the rendering of the Pali is itself contested, is recorded in what_is_disputed rather than hidden. C018 stays primary, with its unprinted four-sphere sum promoted into beat 7 alongside the two abandoned basins, so that the digest's own gap in a count and the reservoir's gap in a count are the same shape. C003 stays for the one-object-at-a-time definition, for the unbroken move through a neck over what is not one thing, and for the two senses of 'one' held apart, with the sources' 'mostly' for the spheres added as a further loose fit between a name and a plural thing. C002 stays for materiality defined by what heat and cold do to it — an earth bund and a cut-stone sluice — and for the fourth reality named in the last beat and refused as unfilmable. The sequence is eight beats, the two_layers and place blocks are rewritten for the new scale, the slate was checked so that this does not repeat the reservoir, irrigation-system or cascade films already on it, and every citation was re-read line by line against its digest: the previous version had C018-M:L3 and C018-M:L125 attached to each other's claims, which is corrected here. Four Commons files were verified through the search API and a titles query before their URLs were written. New aliases added; the title is unchanged.

suggested_location.region: Polonnaruwa District, North Central Province, on the western side of the ancient city of Polonnaruwa; the bund runs along the eastern shore, with the citadel at the northern end and the Potgul Vehera complex at the southern end
suggested_location.why_here: Because the film's argument is here as recorded fact rather than as resemblance. The place is named as a sea and is not one body of water: it was formed by joining separate older reservoirs to each other with narrow channels, and it is counted two ways in print. Five original wewa — Thopa, Dumbutulu, Erabadu, Bhu and Kalahagala — or three interconnected basins today, Thopa, Eramudu and Dumbuthula, because Kalahagala and Bhu were separated from the system and left out of the rehabilitations carried out from 1937. Both counts are correct and neither is a mistake; they count different things, or the same thing at different dates. That is exactly C018's structure, where the tradition counts consciousness as eighty-nine and as a hundred and twenty-one and both are right because they enumerate the same thing at different resolutions. And the only place either count exists is in the air: from the bund or the shore there is one sheet of water and one horizon, which is the supporting concept's one-object-at-a-time with a camera on it. The reservoir then hands the film a second gift the cascade could not — the count visibly changes with the water. At full supply the internal banks are two pale lines; at the bottom of the drawdown they stand clear and the sheet is plainly three. On top of that it delivers the cinema the brief demands: roughly twenty-two square kilometres of shallow water with a flat inland horizon, a fourteen-kilometre earth bund to fly, ancient stone sluices carrying eight centuries of repair in one frame, tens of thousands of waterbirds, and a dead capital and a colossal rock-cut figure standing on the shore at last light.
what_to_film: The high frame on a clear early morning, high enough to hold the whole reservoir with the internal banks legible as lines across it. This is beat 1, beat 5 and beat 8, and the film is built around getting it at both water levels.
One of the necks between basins from directly above, then low and slow through it in a single unbroken move with no cut — the shot beat 6 depends on.
Water level on the bund: lens almost on the surface, a flat horizon, fishing stakes, egrets on a snag, nothing in frame to say how many basins are out there.
The bund flown end to end as one continuous line, roughly fourteen kilometres, with the ruined city on one side and paddy and channels on the other.
The stone sluices close up: cut stone, brick and cement patching, iron fittings, a modern gate set into an ancient opening, and water going out through one of them into a channel.
The drawdown: the margin of cracked grey mud with stumps in it, the shallow arms reduced to channels, and the exposed internal banks that make the three basins visible from the ground for once.

The southern end, where a road on an embankment separates the two basins that were left out, with the outlines of their banks still legible in the scrub and paddy beyond it. This is beat 7 and it must not be dramatised.

Last light at the southern shore: the ruined rotunda and vestibule of the Potgul Vehera library complex and the great rock-cut figure above the water, both as silhouettes against the sheet, then the final lift.
Birds in the shallows in numbers, filmed as the place's own scale rather than as wildlife content.
suggested_location.access: Very easy by comparison with most of the slate. The reservoir is immediately west of the ancient city of Polonnaruwa, reached by the Habarana and Dambulla roads, and the bund road runs along its eastern shore past hotels, the citadel and the Potgul Vehera end. Walking the bund and the shore is straightforward. The complications are permissions, not logistics: the ancient city is a UNESCO World Heritage property administered by the Department of Archaeology and the Central Cultural Fund, the reservoir and its sluices are irrigation works under the Department of Irrigation and the Mahaweli authority, and drone flight over a heritage zone needs civil aviation and site clearance. None of that has been sought and all of it should be treated as the main obstacle to the film.
suggested_location.best_time: Two trips. Roughly February to April, at or soon after full supply, for the single unbroken sheet, the metal sunsets and the bird numbers; then August into September, at the bottom of the irrigation drawdown, for the exposed internal banks, the cracked margins and the shot in which one sheet has become three. Early morning before the dry-zone haze builds for every high frame; the last hour of light for the bund, the sluices and the southern shore. The north-east monsoon, roughly October into January, is the filling period and is worth a reconnaissance but is not needed by any beat.

historical_thread.story: On the western side of the twelfth-century capital of Polonnaruwa lies a reservoir whose name declares it a sea: Parakrama Samudra, the Sea of Parakrama, after Parākramabāhu I, who ruled from Polonnaruwa from 1153 to 1186. It is not a sea and it is not one body of water. The northernmost basin, Thopa Wewa, is far older than the king — reported as built around 386 AD — and what Parākramabāhu did was to enlarge the system and tie separate reservoirs together with narrow channels so that they would function as one storage. Sources describing the original work name five wewa: Thopa, Dumbutulu, Erabadu (also written Eramudu, and called Katu Wewa), Bhu and Kalahagala. Sources describing the reservoir as it is now name three interconnected basins: Thopa, Eramudu and Dumbuthula. The reason for the difference is documented and undramatic. In repair works in the later nineteenth century water that had been reaching Thopa Wewa was redirected towards Bhu Wewa; a temporary dam was built to stop the uncontrolled flow; the temporary dam became a permanent road; and Kalahagala Wewa and Bhu Wewa were thereby cut off from the rest of the network and were not brought back in by the restoration carried out in 1937 and after. What remains is held by an earth bund reported at about fourteen kilometres long and about twelve metres high, with a water surface of roughly twenty-two square kilometres and a maximum depth of about twelve to thirteen metres, serving some eighteen thousand acres of paddy. Along the bund at the southern end stand the ruins of the Potgul Vehera, a monastic complex usually read as a library, and above the water a colossal rock-cut figure. The Cūḷavaṃsa, the Pali chronicle continuing the Mahāvaṃsa, records the injunction for which the king is best remembered: that not even a little of the water that comes from the rain should flow into the ocean without being made useful to man. He is credited in the chronicle with building or restoring 163 major reservoirs, 2,617 minor ones, 3,910 channels, 328 stone sluices and 168 sluice blocks, and with repairing 1,969 breaches in embankments.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: C018's whole point is that a single set of things can be enumerated at two resolutions and that both enumerations are correct: the tradition counts consciousness as eighty-nine and as a hundred and twenty-one, and the difference is only that the eight supramundane types are counted again by the depth of absorption in which they occur, giving forty. Nothing is added by counting more finely. This reservoir is that argument standing in the landscape at a scale a drone can hold in one frame. One name, which says sea, over a thing that is five if you count the reservoirs that were joined and three if you count the basins that hold water together now — two counts that are both in print, that are not in conflict, and that count different things or the same thing at different dates. And the resolution is not a metaphor here: it is literally a question of how much is showing. At full supply the internal banks are two pale lines on the water and the thing reads as one; take a few metres off it in the drawdown and the banks stand clear and it reads as three. The film's best shot is therefore also its clearest statement of the concept, which is what the brief asks for. The digest's own unresolved gap belongs in the same beat as the two abandoned basins: the simple four-sphere sum that would take you from a hundred and twenty-one to eighty-nine is printed in neither source, so even the map's total is partly assembled — and the reservoir's total settled at three because of a temporary dam that became a road. Both are honest gaps in a count, and the film shows them rather than closing them. The supporting concepts are bound by the same geometry. From the bund there is one sheet and one horizon and no count is available at all, which is C003's mind that knows one object at a time and runs as a stream that only seems continuous. And the bund itself, earth piled and stone cut and repeatedly repaired, is C002's materiality defined by what heat and cold and water do to it, while the fourth reality can only be named at the end and not shown.
historical_thread.what_is_certain: The reservoir is on the western side of the ancient city of Polonnaruwa and is named as a sea after Parākramabāhu I, who ruled there 1153–1186. It is not a single basin: it was formed by joining separate reservoirs with narrow channels, and the internal banks still exist. Sources naming the five original wewa give Thopa, Dumbutulu, Erabadu/Eramudu (Katu Wewa), Bhu and Kalahagala. Sources describing it today give three interconnected basins, Thopa, Eramudu and Dumbuthula. Kalahagala and Bhu are outside the present system. A restoration took place in 1937. The Potgul Vehera ruins and a colossal rock-cut figure stand at the southern end of the bund. The Cūḷavaṃsa attributes to the king the injunction about rainwater not reaching the sea, and enumerates his hydraulic works in the figures given above. The reservoir is inside a UNESCO World Heritage property.
historical_thread.what_is_disputed: The count itself is the film's subject and is left open: five and three are both in print and the film does not choose between them. The mechanism of the separation is described consistently but not identically — the redirection of water from Thopa towards Bhu and the temporary dam that became a road are placed in 'the latter 1800s' or 'the nineteenth century' by the popular sources consulted, with the 1937 restoration variously described as the work that fixed the three-basin configuration and as the work in which the old technique of carrying water to all five was mismanaged; no engineering report has been read. The physical figures do not agree: one source gives a surface area of 22.6 km² and a maximum depth of 12.7 m, another gives 5,350 acres (about 21.6 km²) and an average depth of about 25 feet, and the two cannot both be average depth. Attribution is layered rather than settled: the northernmost basin is reported as built around 386 AD, so Parākramabāhu enlarged and joined an existing system rather than creating it from nothing, while several sources simply say he built the reservoir. The Cūḷavaṃsa injunction circulates in several English wordings ('not even a drop of water', 'not even a little water that comes from the rain', 'without benefiting man', 'without being made useful to man'); a chapter-and-verse reference could not be confirmed in this research, and at least one source notes that the Pali behind 'to man' is rendered in Sinhala as lokopakāra, for the benefit of the world, so the film attributes the sentence to the chronicle in general terms and never quotes a verse number. The identification of the colossal figure at the southern end is itself long disputed — the king, the sage Agastya and others have been proposed — and the film records that it is disputed without adjudicating it and without making the figure or the king its subject.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only. The five original wewa and their names, the three interconnected basins counted today, the nineteenth-century redirection of water and the temporary dam that became a road, the 1937 restoration, the exclusion of Kalahagala and Bhu, the bund length and height, the surface area, depths, catchment and irrigated acreage, the presence of the Potgul Vehera and the rock-cut figure, and the Cūḷavaṃsa's injunction and enumeration of works are all from the sources listed above and from the historical_thread's sources; where figures disagree, the disagreement is recorded in what_is_disputed rather than resolved. The coordinates are the reservoir point given in the Wikipedia infobox (7°54′N 80°58′E), rounded, and are an approximate centroid rather than a surveyed position; the bund, the necks between basins, the Potgul Vehera end and the road that cuts off the two abandoned basins have not been located to a coordinate. No chapter-and-verse reference for the chronicle's injunction was confirmed, and no engineering or archaeological report on the rehabilitation history has been read. Access, drone permission over a World Heritage property and over irrigation works, current water level, siltation, weed cover and the state of the sluices are all unverified. The four Commons images were found through the Commons search API and each file's existence, size and licence short-name were confirmed through a titles query before the URLs were written here; all four show the reservoir or the Potgul Vehera ruins themselves rather than a substitute landscape, and none is an aerial, so the film's decisive high frame is not represented by any verified image.

unknowns: No access, permission or local contact has been found or confirmed. Drone clearance over a UNESCO World Heritage property and over active irrigation works is the single largest unknown and could end the film.
Whether the whole reservoir can be held in one frame at a legal drone height, and from where, has not been worked out, and it decides whether the film exists.
Whether the internal banks between the basins are reliably exposed at the bottom of the drawdown, and in which months, has not been checked against irrigation records.
The primary documentation behind the five-and-three counts, and behind the nineteenth-century repair and the 1937 restoration, has not been read; only secondary and popular accounts have.
The exact wording, chapter and verse of the chronicle's injunction, and the best translation of the Pali, are unverified and need an expert reading before anything is spoken.
Whether the necks between the basins can be flown low and clean in a single unbroken move, as beat 6 requires, has not been assessed on the ground.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location was set by Chathura and is not Claude's to change; its supporting detail is desk research and is unverified, and the historical thread separates what is recorded from what is disputed. No scene or shot is decided here.
